subtype: Shares a snack and comforts a friend [Actor]
passage:
Teej swings hung from the neem tree outside the village anganwadi, and all the girls wore green bangles. All except Nirmala, whose bangle had cracked on the swing. She sat by the wall, crying into her knees.
Bhavna looked at her own two biscuits, then at Nirmala. She broke one biscuit in half, sat down close, and held out the bigger piece.
"Here. Don't cry." She patted Nirmala's back, pat, pat, pat, the way Amma did.
Nirmala sniffed and took it. Bhavna leaned her head on Nirmala's shoulder.

qa.q: What happened to Nirmala's bangle?
qa.a: It cracked on the swing.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna share her biscuit and pat Nirmala?
qa.a: She felt sad and caring seeing her friend cry, and wanted Nirmala to feel better, patting her back the way Amma did.

qa.q: How could the anganwadi worker encourage what Bhavna did?
qa.a: Notice it warmly, saying something like "You helped Nirmala feel better," and perhaps help find Nirmala a new bangle.

qa.q: What was it like for Nirmala when Bhavna sat close?
qa.a: Nirmala, crying alone by the wall, likely felt comforted and less alone when Bhavna shared the biscuit and leaned on her.

grounding: A young child breaks her biscuit to share with a crying friend and pats her back.

passage:
"Gargi, you're shivering," Francis said at the classroom door. "Give me your bag."
"It's heavy. My rangoli colours are in it."
"I carry my cricket kit every day. Give."
He slung both bags on, one on each shoulder, and walked her to the auto.
At the gate, Rohit caught up. "What's her rangoli design for the Diwali contest? You know, na? Tell."
"She told me because she trusts me," Francis said.
"Just a hint!"
"Nope."
"Boring."
"Fine. Boring." Francis waved as the auto pulled away. "Get well, Gargi! Your design's locked up safe."
Gargi smiled weakly from the seat. "Knew it would be."

qa.q: What was in Gargi's heavy bag?
qa.a: Her rangoli colours.

qa.q: Why does Francis refuse to give Rohit even a hint?
qa.a: Francis feels loyal and protective of Gargi's trust, since she told him because she trusts him.

qa.q: What would you tell a child pressed to share a friend's surprise like this one?
qa.a: Keeping a harmless surprise, like a rangoli design, is a kind way to honour trust; a secret about someone being hurt, though, should always go to a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel watching Francis from the auto?
qa.a: Gargi, shivering and unwell, likely felt cared for and safe, knowing her bag and her design were in good hands.

grounding: A child carries an ill classmate's bag and keeps the harmless surprise she trusted him with.

passage:
It was Karva Chauth, and back in Jaipur Mummy would be on the terrace with the other aunties, sieve in hand, waiting for the moon. In the Bengaluru flat the power had gone at eight, and Mahima sat on the balcony in the dark, scrolling family photos until her battery hit nine percent. She hadn't told anyone she was sad.
The door creaked. Samir came out with two steel glasses of masala tea and a candle stuck on a saucer.
"You didn't eat dinner," he said, handing her one. He sat on the step beside her and didn't ask anything.
They watched the sky for a while. When the moon finally slid out from behind the clouds, Mahima laughed, a little shakily. "Mummy can eat now."
"Then so can you," Samir said, and passed her a packet of biscuits.

qa.q: What did Samir bring out to the balcony?
qa.a: Two steel glasses of masala tea and a candle stuck on a saucer.

qa.q: How does Mahima feel when Samir sits beside her without asking anything?
qa.a: Mahima, homesick and alone in the dark, likely feels comforted and safe, cared for without having to explain.

qa.q: What made Samir's kindness work so well?
qa.a: He noticed she had skipped dinner, came without being asked, and sat quietly instead of questioning her, letting her share the moment in her own time.

qa.q: What might Samir have noticed that evening?
qa.a: Samir probably noticed that Mahima had skipped dinner and was sitting alone on the balcony, and guessed she was missing home.

grounding: A homesick student on a festival night is brought tea and quiet company by a flatmate and feels she belongs.

passage:
Saturday. Pallavi spent the whole day helping her cousin Tushar move flats: taping boxes, haggling with the tempo driver, scrubbing the new kitchen. That evening she still dropped dinner at Nani's.
Tuesday. She got home at ten after a twelve-hour shift at the hospital billing desk, feet throbbing. Tushar called. "Can you come over and help me with the gas connection form? Tonight?"
Pallavi closed her eyes. The old Pallavi would have grabbed her keys. "Not tonight, Tushar. I'm completely wiped out. Thursday after seven, I'm all yours."
A pause. "Okay. Thursday."
Thursday. Rested, she filled the form in fifteen minutes, and they ate instant noodles on his new balcony, laughing about the tempo driver.

qa.q: What time did Pallavi get home on Tuesday?
qa.a: At ten, after a twelve-hour shift at the hospital billing desk.

qa.q: What did Pallavi feel when Tushar asked for help on Tuesday night?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and torn, closing her eyes as the old habit pulled her toward saying yes.

qa.q: Why did saying no on Tuesday turn out to be kind as well?
qa.a: Resting let her help properly on Thursday, finishing the form in fifteen minutes and enjoying the evening, instead of helping while empty and resentful.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt during the pause after her no?
qa.a: Tushar may have felt surprised or a bit disappointed, since she usually said yes, but he agreed and got better help on Thursday.

grounding: An adult helps her cousin generously but says no when exhausted, offering a later time instead.

passage:
PT note, Holi week, Class 5. Sarika
During kho-kho today, the captains picked every child except Chaoba, who joined us from Imphal last month. One boy said, "He talks funny, he won't understand the rules." Chaoba stood by the fence, pretending to tie his shoe.
Before I could step in, Farida walked out of her team's line. "That's not fair. He runs faster than all of you. And he's in our class, same as us." Her voice was shaking, but she didn't sit down.
I asked Farida's team if Chaoba could take the first chase. He tagged three players out. From tomorrow I will rotate the teams so nobody is left standing, and I will speak with the captains.

qa.q: How many players did Chaoba tag out?
qa.a: Three players.

qa.q: How did Farida feel speaking up, and what shows it?
qa.a: Farida felt nervous but sure it was unfair; her voice shook, yet she didn't sit down.

qa.q: What did the PT teacher do next, and why does it help?
qa.a: The teacher gave Chaoba the first chase, planned rotating teams so nobody is left standing, and will speak with the captains, making fairness part of the routine.

qa.q: What was it like for Chaoba standing by the fence?
qa.a: Chaoba likely felt hurt and embarrassed, pretending to tie a shoe to hide being left out, until Farida spoke up.

grounding: A child objects when a classmate from another state is left out of a game and says it is unfair.

passage:
15 August, night
Flag hoisting in the morning, then the colony tree drive. Yash and I planted three neem saplings by the drain road, muddy up to our elbows. Aunty from B-block said, "Why bother, the municipality will cut them." I watered them anyway.
Then tonight on the news, the floods up north. A whole village under water, people on rooftops with their goats. I don't know anyone there. But I can't stop thinking about them. Same rain, same sky, and our drains are choked with plastic too. It all feels connected and too big, and I'm angry that grown-ups just shrug.
Tomorrow I'll ask Sir if our class can collect clothes for the relief drive. And I'll check on the neems.
Alka

qa.q: How many neem saplings did Alka and Yash plant?
qa.a: Three neem saplings, by the drain road.

qa.q: How does Alka feel after seeing the floods on the news?
qa.a: Alka feels worried, angry and a bit overwhelmed, thinking about strangers on rooftops and how the same rain and choked drains link them to home.

qa.q: What small steps is Alka planning, and why do they help?
qa.a: Asking Sir about a class clothes collection for the relief drive and checking on the neems; small local acts give a big worry somewhere to go.

qa.q: How might Aunty from B-block see the tree drive?
qa.a: Aunty sees it as pointless, expecting the municipality to cut the trees, and may not share Alka's sense that small acts matter.

grounding: A teenager plants trees and worries about distant flood victims, sensing how the world is linked.

subtype: Universal principle against loyalty to own circle [Actor]
passage:
The hostel office had a paper star hanging for Christmas when Zeenat found Pema alone with the room-allotment sheet.
"You're on the committee," Zeenat whispered. "Just put me in C-block. The one with working geysers. Nobody will know."
Pema looked at the list. Eighty names, a lottery drawn in front of everyone last week. Zeenat was number sixty-two, which meant the old block with the leaking roof. Zeenat, who had sat by Pema's hospital bed for three nights in first year.
"I can't change the list," Pema said slowly. "It isn't fair to the other seventy-nine."
Zeenat's face fell.
Pema's chest ached. "But I'll go with you to the warden tomorrow about the roof. And my heater is yours all winter."
Zeenat didn't answer. But she didn't leave, either.

qa.q: What number was Zeenat on the list?
qa.a: Number sixty-two.

qa.q: How did Pema feel refusing Zeenat's request?
qa.a: Pema felt torn and pained, chest aching, loyal to the friend who sat by that hospital bed yet unwilling to be unfair to the other seventy-nine.

qa.q: How did Pema work through the tension instead of choosing carelessly?
qa.a: Pema kept the fair lottery but offered real help inside it: going to the warden about the roof and sharing a heater all winter.

qa.q: What might Zeenat be feeling as she stays without answering?
qa.a: Zeenat is likely hurt and disappointed, but staying suggests she may understand, or at least is not ending the friendship.

grounding: A young adult is torn between a fair lottery and a close friend's request, and finds a way to help within the rules.

subtype: Turning wide concern into local action [Response]
passage: Irfan, you asked why I spend Sunday mornings at the ward library. At twenty-four I used to argue about big things all night: equality, climate, the whole world. Then one Sunday old Mrs Fernandes from the ground floor, who couldn't read the small print on her ration form, asked me for help, and I said I was busy. She went to the neighbour's son instead, a Class 9 boy. I felt small that day. So I started simply. I filled forms for anyone in our lane every Sunday, whoever came, whatever their faith. I read every candidate's papers properly before each election instead of voting by habit. I learned the names of the sweepers. Nobody wrote about it. But twenty years on, the lane still calls me Form-wala Mridul.

qa.q: What did Mrs Fernandes need help with?
qa.a: Reading the small print on her ration form.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel after saying no to Mrs Fernandes?
qa.a: Mridul felt small and ashamed, having argued about equality all night but being too busy to help the neighbour downstairs.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what came of it?
qa.a: Saying no to Mrs Fernandes and seeing a Class 9 boy help instead; after that Mridul filled forms for anyone every Sunday and began voting with care.

qa.q: How might Mrs Fernandes have felt when the Class 9 boy helped instead?
qa.a: She was probably relieved to get the help, and perhaps a little hurt that the grown neighbour had said no.

grounding: An elder recalls turning big ideals into small steady acts: filling neighbours' forms, voting with care and respecting everyone.

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage:
The sports club's winter carnival had a new climbing wall, three storeys of coloured holds, and Ayesha had spotted it from the gate.
"Himani Ma'am, please, please can I go first?" She was already bouncing on her toes.
"It's the tallest one. Are you sure? The small wall is open too."
"The small wall is for babies. I did it last year. It's so boring." Ayesha tugged at her harness strap. "Please! What if I can reach the top?"
Himani Ma'am checked the harness twice and clipped the rope. Ayesha scrambled up, knees scraping, heart racing, and slapped the bell at the top. It rang across the whole club.
"Next!" she shouted down. "What's next?"

qa.q: How tall was the new climbing wall?
qa.a: Three storeys of coloured holds.

qa.q: Why does Ayesha call the small wall boring?
qa.a: She feels bored by what she has already done and excited by anything new and hard, so the tallest wall feels far more alive than the safe one.

qa.q: How did Himani Ma'am balance Ayesha's thirst for thrills with safety?
qa.a: She checked the harness twice and clipped the rope, letting Ayesha take the challenge with protection in place.

qa.q: How might Himani Ma'am feel hearing Ayesha shout "What's next?"
qa.a: Himani Ma'am probably feels amused and a little tired, seeing that one thrill only makes Ayesha hungry for the next.

grounding: A child begs to climb the tallest wall because anything familiar feels boring and new challenges feel thrilling.

subtype: Conformity: follows rules to avoid upsetting others [Actor]
passage:
Monday, Annual Day month. Bhavna lined up first, shirt tucked, ribbons tied in two loops exactly like Nandini's and the others'. When the teacher left the room, she still kept her finger on her lips.
Wednesday. Nandini asked the group, "Class play: fairy tale or space?" Bhavna's heart jumped at space; she had a whole story about a girl on Mars. But everyone said fairy tale. "Fairy tale," Bhavna said quickly.
Friday. Ma'am asked, "Bhavna, you're quiet. What would you like the play to be?"
"Whatever everyone likes, Ma'am."
That night she drew a rocket at the back of her rough notebook, then shut it before Mummy could see.

qa.q: What did Bhavna say when Ma'am asked for her choice on Friday?
qa.a: "Whatever everyone likes, Ma'am."

qa.q: Why did Bhavna say "Fairy tale" when she wanted space?
qa.a: She was afraid of standing out or being disapproved of, so she buried her excitement about her Mars story to match the group.

qa.q: How could Ma'am help Bhavna share her own ideas?
qa.a: Collect ideas on paper or one by one so nobody sees the others' votes, and welcome different answers warmly, so Bhavna feels safe to say space.

qa.q: What would change if Nandini had asked Bhavna first?
qa.a: Bhavna might have felt safe to say space before hearing the group, and the class might have heard her Mars story.

grounding: A child follows every rule and copies the group's choices, burying her own wish for a space play.
